name: Oirats and the Dzungar Khanate
summary: Western Mongol peoples who formed the Four Oirat confederation, captured a Ming emperor (1449) and later built the Dzungar Khanate, the last great steppe empire, destroyed by the Qing in 1755–58.

knownFor.label: Galdan Boshugtu
knownFor.note: Dzungar khan who fought the Qing.

knownFor.label: Kalmyks
knownFor.note: Oirats who moved to the Volga (1630s).

location.value: At its greatest extent from southern Siberia to Tibet, with its core in northern Xinjiang (Dzungaria); 3,600,000 km² in 1650 (infobox).

terrain.value: Steppe, the Altai and Tian Shan mountains and desert basins.

climate.value: Very continental: bitter winters and dry summers.

resources.value: Horses, sheep, cattle and camels; some farming in the Ili valley.

disasters.value: Harsh winters (dzud); smallpox; the Qing campaigns (1755–58).

population.value: About 600,000 people in 200,000 households before the Qing conquest, per the Qing scholar Wei Yuan.

urbanisation.value: Mostly nomadic; Ghulja in the Ili valley was the Dzungar centre.

disease.value: Smallpox epidemics in the 1750s devastated the population.

migration.value: Some Oirats (the Kalmyks) moved to the Volga in the 1630s.

economicBase.value: Mainly animal herding with limited farming; the Dzungars mined iron, copper and silver and made firearms, and after conquering the Yarkent Khanate in 1680 used Tarim Basin people as forced farm labour.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with Russia, China and Central Asia.

wealth.value: Herds and tribute from subject peoples.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute from subject peoples and caravan trade.

inequality.value: Rulers and military elites above farmers and herders.

governmentType.value: A confederation of four Oirat tribes (Choros, Torghut, Dörbet, Khoid), later the Dzungar Khanate.

keyRulers.value: Esen Taishi (r. 1439–1455); Galdan Boshugtu ruled 1671–1697, took the title in 1678, conquered the Tarim Basin in 1680 and was defeated by the Qing in 1696; Galdan Tseren succeeded Tsewang Rabtan in 1727 and died in 1745.

succession.value: Contested between princes, often by murder.

institutions.value: Assemblies of nobles; the Mongol-Oirat law code (1640).

stability.value: Strong under great khans, collapsing in succession wars.

eliteConflict.value: Rival princes competed for the khanate.

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry; the Dzungars cast cannon with Swedish prisoners’ help.

majorWars.value: The Qing destroyed the khanate within about 100 days in 1755. Wei Yuan estimated 40% of households died of smallpox, 20% fled and 30% were killed; another account says 80% of over 600,000 people were destroyed; historians describe the campaign as genocide.

territoryChange.value: Took Tibet (1717) and Kazakh lands; lost everything to the Qing (1755–58).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals of the Qing, the Khalkha Mongols and the Kazakhs.

religion.value: The Oirats converted to Tibetan Buddhism in 1615, and a legal code of 1640 supported the Gelug sect.

languageWriting.value: Oirat Mongolian, written in the Clear Script created by Zaya Pandita (1648).

sharedIdentity.value: An Oirat (western Mongol) identity, set against the eastern Mongols and the Qing.

dailyLife.value: Families lived in felt tents (ger) and ate meat and dairy.

neighbours.value: Qing China, Khalkha Mongols, Kazakhs, Russia, Tibet.

ideasReligions.value: Tibetan Buddhism shaped politics and ritual.

riseSignals.value: Dzungar Khanate established in 1634 (infobox) by Erdeni Batur on the upper Emil River.

peakPeriod.value: Territorial apex about 1717, after the conquest of Tibet.

declineSignals.value: A succession war after 1745 weakened the khanate before the Qing conquest.

outcome.value: From 1755 to 1758 the Qing conquered Dzungaria, destroying the khanate within 100 days of 1755 and killing most Dzungars; the infobox gives a population of 600,000–1,200,000.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles; population figures are estimates.
